title: What They Said About the Project
summary: After the group project presentations, Omar told his father about what his teammates had said.
text:
After the group project presentations, Omar told his father about what his teammates had said.
"Sara said that she had enjoyed painting the buildings," Omar reported. "And she said that the details which she added made the model look realistic."
His father smiled. "You're using reported speech and relative clauses correctly," he observed. "You said 'Sara said that she had enjoyed' — that's reported speech with backshift. And you said 'the details which she added' — that's a relative clause describing the details."
Omar nodded. "Youssef said that he would design the roads tomorrow. And he said that the power grid which he planned would be solar-powered."
"Perfect," said his father. "You said 'he would design' — that's reported speech with future-in-the-past. And 'the power grid which he planned' — that's another relative clause."
That evening, Adam told his mother about the project too. "Ms. Rania said that the team which had collaborated best would win," he reported. "And she said that our team had won because we had divided tasks by strength."
"Excellent," said his mother. "You're using reported speech with past perfect ('she had won,' 'we had divided') and relative clauses ('the team which had collaborated') correctly. That's advanced grammar."
Adam smiled. "I'm going to keep practicing," he said. "Because I think it will help me communicate more clearly."
"That's exactly right," said his mother. "Reported speech helps you communicate what others have said accurately. Relative clauses help you describe people and things precisely. And future forms help you talk about plans and predictions. You're using all three structures naturally now."
Adam felt proud. He hadn't realized he was using three grammar structures at once — but now that he knew, he noticed them everywhere.
lesson: Reported speech helps you communicate accurately what others have said; relative clauses help you describe people and things precisely; future forms help you talk about plans and predictions; using all three structures together makes your communication clearer, more accurate, and more specific — and you're already using them naturally.

title: The Essay That Was Written
summary: Layla was proud of the essay she had written.
text:
Layla was proud of the essay she had written.
"The essay was graded yesterday," she told her father. "And it was praised by Ms. Rania."
His father raised an eyebrow. "You're using passive voice," he observed. "You said 'the essay was graded' and 'it was praised' — focusing on the action, not on who did it."
Layla nodded. "I also used gerunds and infinitives. I wrote, 'I enjoy writing essays,' and 'I decided to study harder.' And I used discourse markers too: 'However, writing is challenging.' 'Therefore, I practice daily.' 'Furthermore, I seek feedback.'"
His father smiled. "You're using all three structures correctly," he said. "Passive voice for focus on the action ('was graded,' 'was praised'). Gerunds after 'enjoy' ('enjoy writing'). Infinitives after 'decided' ('decided to study'). And discourse markers for structured thinking ('however,' 'therefore,' 'furthermore')."
"That's a lot," said Layla.
"It is," agreed her father. "But you're using them naturally in your speech and writing. You just didn't know the grammar names for them."
That evening, Layla told her mother about the essay. "The feedback which I received was helpful," she reported. "And I'm going to apply it to my next essay."
"Perfect," said her mother. "You said 'the feedback which I received' — that's a relative clause. And 'I'm going to apply' — that's future with 'going to' for a plan. You're using all the grammar structures we've learned — passive voice, gerunds and infinitives, discourse markers, relative clauses, and future forms — correctly and naturally."
Layla felt proud. She had learned something important: grammar isn't just rules — it's tools for clear, precise communication. And she was using those tools skillfully.
lesson: Passive voice helps you focus on the action rather than the actor; gerunds and infinitives help you express preferences and decisions naturally; discourse markers help you structure your thinking and writing clearly; grammar isn't just abstract rules — it's practical tools for clear, precise communication, and you're already using them skillfully.
